synopsis: A program starting in October 2026 can realistically have a parameterized machine-and-brake model working by mid-2027; an executable SIL regression framework on that schedule is conditional on defining software interfaces [f67, f840]. Off-road braking follows the same underlying physics as road braking, but machine dynamics, ground interaction and brake response do not transfer automatically from road vehicles or between machine families [f5886, f1731, f10430]. Models must account for payload, articulation, terrain interaction, brake capability and latency, while ground-induced changes in machine attitude also change sensor pose; even perfect sensor simulation cannot compensate for incorrect braking dynamics [f3971, f3959, f5089]. SIL and modeled-machine HIL cannot establish true machine behavior, while VIL can demonstrate real braking and delays but may omit soft soil, grades and other important conditions; physical stopping tests should therefore bound models for each machine family and surface class [f926, f5287, f5333, f5336, f10612]. The recommended approach layers fast threshold, stability and selective high-fidelity models, with separate validation and uncertainty reporting: greater complexity is not automatically greater credibility, as a 2026 on-road round robin reported spreads of 0.033 s and 0.314 m for more complex models, and NIOSH's 2018 stopping model still required validation [f13060, f10617, f5907, f5949].

relations.note: Both identify false interventions as human-factors and vehicle-dynamics hazards.
Uncompared models remain hypotheses rather than evidence.
Both reject automatic transfer of dynamics, brakes and sensing between machine families.
Sensor simulation cannot establish safety when machine braking dynamics are wrong.
Adds executable regression scope and an interface-definition condition to the mid-2027 forecast.
Nontransferable physical content motivates separate qualification of dynamics and brake models.
Elevated payload changes dynamics, supporting explicit mass, inertia and payload transfer parameters.
Ground-induced attitude changes provide a specific mechanism linking dynamics to sensor data.
SIL's inability to establish true dynamics also applies when HIL retains modeled machinery.
Qualifies VIL's braking evidence with conditions its bench may not reproduce.
Potential VIL terrain omissions motivate physical stopping tests by family and surface.
Details speed and pose updates and regenerated controller feedback after the replay branch.
Intervention replay requires adequately recorded machine state and brake commands.
Simulated downhill non-stopping cases reinforce the need for physical bounds on model predictions.
Extensive stopping-model parameter sweeps still required validation, illustrating simulation's evidentiary limits.
Complex-model variability supports reserving high-fidelity models for selected challenges to simpler models.
Equivalence must show extreme variants bound intermediates despite non-monotonic geometry and braking effects.
Extends uncertainty separation into explicit verification and validation reporting for physical and timing components.
